Fron0ers ar0cle, The Poten0al for Lunar and Mar0an Regolith Simulants to Sustain Plant Growth: A 
Mul0disciplinary Overview, “The addi0on of compost to pure (Mar0an) simulant propor0onally

Theory 
Addi0ves to Mar0an regolith can help increase water reten0on and plant growth in Mar0an crops. A 
light weight, low volume regolith addi0ve would be beneﬁcial to a future mission to Mars. We 
hypothesize that compressed French sponges (cellulose), dried and compressed peat moss, and clay 
pebbles will increase water reten0on and plant growth in Mar0an crops while minimizing increases to 
mission payloads. 
Compressed French sponges are very small and light weight. They are made of natural cellulose, and we 
hope they will help to decrease the density of the Mar0an regolith while also increasing water reten0on. 
Dried and compressed peat moss is very light weight and takes up slightly more volume than 
compressed sponges. We hope peat moss will decrease the density of Mar0an regolith, while increasing 
water reten0on. Peat moss may also have the beneﬁt of adding more nutrients to the regolith. Peat 
moss is a large source of stored carbon on earth and expor0ng carbon in large quan00es may warrant 
further studies. 
Clay beads are light weight but do take up the most volume. We chose to include them because of their 
porousness. We hope they will decrease the density of the Mar0an simulant and improve water ﬂow 
and reten0on.

Discussion and Conclusions 
Earth and Mars Controls The earth control pots were vastly diﬀerent from the Mars control pots in both 
plan0ngs. Seedlings did not grow in the Mars control pots at all. One seed germinated, but it did not 
produce any roots or shoots. This is likely because of the salt, which was visible on the surface of the 
simulant, (Figure 6) and the very low pH levels (5.25 pH) measured in the pots (Figure 7). The earth 
control pots had a normal range of pH levels (7.5 pH) and were able to grow many seedlings. 
The Mars pots lost the most water over the 3-day measurement period (Graph 7). The earth pots did not 
have the highest water reten0on but was s0ll much beeer than the Mars pots. It is likely that the earth 
pots would have had a higher water reten0on if the water was not being used by the germina0ng seeds 
and seedlings. We found the results to be very similar in plan0ng 2. 
Figure 6: Salts in Mar0an simulant 
 
 
Figure 7: pH earth (le`) and Mars (right) 
 
Clay Pebbles We decided to try clay pebbles as an addi0ve to retain water because they are o`en used 
in hydroponics and are very absorbent. No seedlings sprouted above the surface during the experiment. 
One seed germinated, but it did not produce any roots or shoots. However, while cleaning out the pots 
at the end of the experiment, we found many seedlings had germinated, produced, roots, shoots and 
grown inside the hollows of the clay pebbles beneath the Mar0an regolith surface (Figure 8). The 
seedlings were not able to grow into the Mar0an regolith, possibly because of the acidic condi0ons of 
the simulant. The seedlings twisted around inside of the clay pebbles to grow within the hollow. 
We were surprised that the clay pebbles did not retain water as we had expected. As you can see in 
Graph 7, they lost more water than they were watered with a`er 3 days. However, they did not lose as 
much water on average as the Mar0an pots. We found the results to be very similar in plan0ng 2.

Peat Moss The peat moss pots had the best seedling results in the Mar0an regolith soil for all data 
points (Table 2). Although the Mars pots were able to grow seedlings, the roots stayed in the peat moss 
and did not root into Mars soil. This resulted in the roots becoming a glob within the moss. The peat 
moss and radish plant came out of the container in a square shape (Figure 10). We also determined that 
the peat moss would not be easy to transport to Mars because of the amount needed and the space it 
would take up on the shuele. 
Peat moss did retain more water than the earth control pots (Graph 7). This could possibly be explained 
by the higher numbers of seedlings taking water from the earth pots than the peat moss pots. 
We did not plant any peat moss pots in the second plan0ng. We wanted to try another addi0ve (orbee 
water beads) and did not have enough Mar0an simulant to test both. 
Figure 10 and 11: Seedling roots in peat moss harves0ng 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Sponge The sponge pots in plan0ng 1 did not show any signiﬁcant growth. 1 seedling germinated a`er 
7 days but did not grow roots or sprout. No growth was discovered at harvest beneath the soil either. 
However, in plan0ng 2 the sponges were placed on top of the regolith, instead of beneath, this led to the 
germina0on and growth of 8 seedlings in 1 pot (Table 3, Figure 12). The seedlings grew within the 
sponge but stopped growing when the roots reached the Mar0an regolith. The seedlings reached a 
maximum height of 4 cm. 
The sponge pots retained the most water 3 days a`er being watered (Graph 7). 
Figure 12: Sponges beneath soil in Plan0ng 1 and on top of soil in Plan0ng 2

9 
 
Orbee Water Beads For plan0ng 2, we decided to test another addi0ve instead of peat moss. We were 
hopeful that water beads would absorb and hold water, then release the water as the regolith began to 
dry. No seeds germinated in these pots. It is possible that the compactness and heaviness of the Mar0an 
regolith did not allow the water beads to expand. Further tes0ng needs to be done to make any 
conclusions about the water beads. We did not have enough Mar0an simulant to adequately test this 
addi0ve. No mass measurements were taken for these pots. 
Other Findings Seedlings did not grow directly in the Mar0an soil. The seedling roots did their best to 
stay within addi0ves like peat moss, sponge or clay beads to avoid the salty, acidic Mar0an regolith. 
However, the microorganism, pictured below (Figures 13 and 14) grew very well on the Mar0an 
simulant. This would be an interes0ng organism to research in the future. 
Figure 13: Microorganism growing in Mar0an regolith 
Figure 14: Microorganism at 40x magniﬁca0on 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Conclusion Red Arrow Heirloom microgreen radish seeds do not grow directly in the Mar0an regolith 
simulant provided. This is likely a consequence of the salty and acidic proper0es of the Mar0an regolith. 
The seeds did germinate within addi0ves (sponge pieces, clay pebbles and peat moss) but growth of the 
seedlings stopped as soon as the roots began to grow directly into the regolith soil. More research is 
needed on ways to improve these condi0ons within Mar0an regolith. 
Sponge pieces and peat moss greatly increased the water reten0on of the Mar0an regolith. Clay beads 
also increased the water reten0on of the regolith but were s0ll losing more water than they were 
receiving. This is probably due to the hollow centers of the pebbles. 
The addi0ves may also be helping to aerate the Mar0an regolith. Without the addi0ves, the regolith was 
much more compact and dense. 
Another area that would be exci0ng to research would be the microorganisms that ﬂourish on the 
Mar0an regolith. It may be possible to ﬁnd a microorganism that can improve the pH and salt content of 
the regolith as a byproduct of its’ growth.
